title: The Rented Hall: Dresden, Buenos Aires, and the Last Solo of Ausdruckstanz
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Dresden, born in a mason's household
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Neue Deutsche Biographie, the Sächsische Biografie and the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln give 12 December 1911 independently. Coordinate is the corpus's general Dresden pin, inherited from mary_wigman.journey.json; the birth address is not recorded in any reachable source.
stops.campa: A fourth child is born in Dresden on the twelfth of December and registered as Dore Hoyer. Her father Hermann Gustav Hoyer cuts stone; her mother Anna Amalia, born Pöpperl, keeps the house. There is no money in it for the kind of training the century is just then inventing, and no reason yet to want any. She will spend fifty-six years inside that argument and never hold a company of her own for longer than three seasons. The city she is born into is already the capital of the new German dance, its schools filling with women who mean to make the body speak without telling a story.
suggested_refs: Dresden civil registration of December 1911; the Hoyer family papers in Bestand 001, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden-Blasewitz, the school of Ilse Homilius
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, month unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the centre of Blasewitz; the background dossier's 51.0311/13.7897 lands in Strehlen. The Dalcroze derivation of the curriculum is reconstruction, not attested.
stops.campa: In Blasewitz, east of the Elbe bridges, Ilse Homilius keeps a school for rhythm, music and bodily formation, and takes the seventeen-year-old in as a scholarship pupil. The method is said to descend from Emile Jaques-Dalcroze by way of Hellerau and Laxenburg: counting made physical, music entered through the feet before it is entered through the ear. Hoyer arrives at dance through the back door of pedagogy, and never through ballet at all. A schoolteacher had already found free gymnastics lessons for her at twelve, the family having nothing to spend on such things.
suggested_refs: The Hellerau-Laxenburg rhythmics curriculum, from which Homilius's Blasewitz syllabus is said to descend
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, the teacher's diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is inferred from the usual examination season and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Lingnerplatz 1 from the dossier's 51.0533/13.7625.
stops.campa: At the Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, the great white house of the healthy body, Homilius's pupils perform in front of an audience that has come to look at anatomy. Hoyer takes her diploma the same year, in pedagogy and gymnastics, qualified to instruct in schools. It is a certificate to earn a living with, and she means to earn a living with it. She will be back on this floor five years later with a dead man's music. Nothing on the paper says dancer.
suggested_refs: The Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, Lingnerplatz 1, Dresden, performance venue of the Homilius school
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, the year at Palucca's school
stops.date_confidence: attested for the academic year 1930/31; the month is a convention for the term's start. The premises are unlocated: the present Palucca Hochschule building at Basteiplatz dates from 1952-55, and Palucca's earlier rooms are undocumented, so the general Dresden pin stands in.
stops.campa: Gret Palucca has broken away from Mary Wigman to teach a dance of her own in Dresden, and Hoyer enrols for a single year. Her teacher there is Irma Steinberg, who declines to hand her a system and tells her to find her own; the school's jumping, high and dry and weightless, stays in her legs for good. At the end of it she sits the dance examination. Where the rooms stood in 1930 nobody wrote down: Palucca taught first out of her own flat by the Bürgerwiese, then in rented halls whose address has not survived.
suggested_refs: Gret Palucca's Dresden school and its jumping technique, taught by Irma Steinberg in 1930/31
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Plauen, a season of operetta
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1931-32 season; the month is the conventional season opening and is defaulted.
stops.campa: The examination is barely cold when Plauen engages her as its solo dancer for the season. The Vogtland town wants operetta: a dance inserted between numbers, a girl in a costume, three minutes of charm and off again. Whatever she has been trained to look for is not in the second act of an operetta. By the end of the season she has worked out that the theatres will not give her the thing she wants, and that the evenings she wants will have to be made by hand. She does the year out anyway.
suggested_refs: The Stadttheater Plauen and its 1931-32 operetta repertoire
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, the composer at the piano
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Back in Dresden she meets Peter Cieslak, eighteen years old, a musician who composes. He becomes her lover, her household, her pianist and the only collaborator she will ever describe as an equal. For three years Hoyer has the working method she will spend the remaining thirty-two years failing to rebuild. They work as a single apparatus: he writes the score, she makes the dance to it, the two things invented together in one room rather than one fitted over the other afterwards.
suggested_refs: Peter Cieslak's manuscript scores in Bestand 001, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Künstlerhaus Dresden, the first evening of their own
stops.date_confidence: date attested exactly by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln. Venue doubtful: the archive names the Künstlerhaus without an address, and the only Dresden building of that name is the studio house at Pillnitzer Landstrasse in Loschwitz, used here and flagged. The dossier's 51.058/13.744 matched no building of the name.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of March, eight weeks after the Reichstag burns, Hoyer and Cieslak rent a hall and give their first evening on their own account. She is twenty-one. The programme carries Ernste Gesänge, her setting of Brahms's late songs of death, and the public comes and stays. It is the first spring of a state that will spend twelve years deciding what a German body is permitted to express. The audience in the rented hall is her own, assembled outside every theatre in the city.
suggested_refs: Ernste Gesänge, after Brahms's Vier ernste Gesänge, premiered 30 March 1933
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Oldenburg, ballet mistress for a salary
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1933-34 season; the month is the conventional season opening and is defaulted.
stops.campa: Oldenburg's Landestheater takes her on as Tanzmeisterin for the season, and the post is what such posts are: dance inserts for opera and operetta, cut to the house's measure, paid monthly. The arrangement is one she will repeat all her life, a season inside an institution to pay for the seasons outside it. She takes this one to keep Cieslak composing. Two hundred and fifty miles north of Dresden she spends a year staging other people's interludes, then comes back south with the salary spent and nothing from the year worth keeping.
suggested_refs: The Landestheater Oldenburg season books for 1933-34

stops.name: Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, five dances with no names
stops.date_confidence: attested for February 1935 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. The 1934 evening at the Komödie is folded into this stop because that theatre's historical address could not be established.
stops.campa: A second solo evening has already come and gone at the Komödie; the third is here, in February, and its centre is Cieslak's Fünf namenlose Tänze, five dances with no names. He plays, she dances what he wrote. The museum that watched her take a teacher's diploma five years earlier watches the last work the two of them make together. Nothing in the programme, and nothing written down afterwards about the evening, suggests that either of them knew what February was. Six weeks later he is dead.
suggested_refs: Fünf namenlose Tänze, music by Peter Cieslak, February 1935
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, the death of Peter Cieslak
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln. The place of his death is not given in any reachable source; the general Dresden pin stands in.
stops.campa: On the fifth of April Peter Cieslak kills himself. Where, and for what reason, the record does not say. Hoyer holds herself responsible and, not long after, attempts the same thing and survives it. The partnership that made the evenings possible is gone, the composer is gone, and the way of working she had built with him has no second person left in it. The months that follow are empty in the record; when it resumes she is standing in a rehearsal room that belongs to somebody else. She is twenty-three.
suggested_refs: Hoyer's own 1935 suicide attempt, recorded in the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln estate biography
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, asking Mary Wigman for the group
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1935; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. That she joined as a company dancer and not as a pupil is attested; de.wikipedia's Mary Wigman article states she 'war jedoch nie ihre Schülerin'.
stops.campa: In September she goes to Mary Wigman and asks to be taken into the new group. Wigman takes her, and the terms are exact and will matter for thirty years: Hoyer joins as a dancer in the company, not as a pupil in the school. Half the literature will make her Wigman's disciple regardless; the German record says plainly that she never was one. Through the autumn she rehearses Tanzgesänge among women who have been formed in Wigman's method for years, and she has not been.
suggested_refs: Frank-Manuel Peter's dissertation on Hoyer, FU Berlin, which the background dossier credited with rejecting the pupil narrative; unreachable behind a bot-block
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, Tanzgesänge and the northern tour
stops.date_confidence: attested by the NDB, the Sächsische Biografie and the Tanzarchiv independently; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. Gap: no reachable source names the festival's host city or any single stop on the tour, only the four countries, so the Dresden pin holds the whole episode.
stops.campa: Tanzgesänge premieres at the November Tanzfestspiele and then goes on the road: Germany first, then the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, into the following spring. Which cities took the piece, and in what order, no reachable source preserves. Hoyer is inside a large group work for the first and nearly the last time, one body among many, moving to somebody else's design. It is also the first time she is paid to cross a border. She is twenty-four and has never before worked outside Germany.
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman's Tanzgesänge, premiered November 1935 and toured through Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and Sweden
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, Wiatowitsch and the rented halls
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1936 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which is sharper than the background dossier's bare 1936; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. The self-financing under the concert agencies' resistance is attested from about 1937.
stops.campa: In May she leaves the group and takes up solo work again, and finds the second musician of her life: Dimitri Wiatowitsch, pianist, percussionist and composer, who will accompany her for thirty years and write the scores of her last great cycles. The National Socialist concert agencies want nothing to do with the kind of evening she makes, all darkness and single figures and no uplift, so she rents the halls herself, at her own risk, and sells the tickets herself. It is the arrangement she will die inside.
suggested_refs: Dimitri Wiatowitsch's scores for Hoyer, including Affectos Humanos, in Bestand 001, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Berlin, the Deutsche Tanzbühne
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1940-41 by the NDB and the Tanzarchiv; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Gap: no reachable source names the Berlin house, so a declared central Berlin coordinate is used.
stops.campa: Hanns Niedecken-Gebhardt assembles a Deutsche Tanzbühne for Joseph Goebbels's ministry, and Hoyer dances in it. She takes the engagement because there is work in it, in a profession whose alternative is renting halls nobody will license you to fill. What she danced in Berlin under that management, no programme in reach records. The company is a state instrument and does not last: within the year it is dissolved and reconstituted as a troupe for entertaining the Wehrmacht. She does not follow it there.
suggested_refs: The Deutsche Tanzbühne under Hanns Niedecken-Gebhardt, 1940-41, and its reconstitution as a Wehrmacht entertainment troupe
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, two seasons at the Theater des Volkes
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which records the engagement on the dissolution of the Tanzbühne in 1941; the month is the conventional season opening. The theatre's exact address is approximate.
stops.campa: The Tanzbühne dissolved, Dresden's Theater des Volkes engages Hoyer as its soloist and keeps her two seasons. Wartime entertainment policy wants cheer, so the dance is small and decorative and folded inside operettas, and the woman who had set Brahms's songs of death to a body standing alone performs them because they are the engagement. She has no evenings of her own in these years, no company of her own, and no agency in the country that will book her an evening. Two seasons pass this way.
suggested_refs: The wartime repertoire of the Theater des Volkes, Dresden, 1941-43
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Graz, the last wartime season
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1943-44 season by the Tanzarchiv, the NDB and the Sächsische Biografie; the month is the conventional season opening and is defaulted.
stops.campa: Karl Bergeest, ballet master at Graz, takes her south into Austria as soloist for what turns out to be the last wartime season the Stadttheater plays. In September 1944 the theatres shut by order and the personnel are conscripted into war production; the season she has just finished is the last engagement of her career under the old dispensation. Styria in 1943 is still a place where an opera house runs to schedule and the front is a bulletin on the radio.
suggested_refs: The Stadttheater Graz under ballet master Karl Bergeest, season 1943-44
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, forced labour at Zeiss Ikon
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1944 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which sharpens the background dossier's '1944-1945'; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. The branch is unnamed in every reachable source, so the Ernemann works at Schandauer Strasse 76 stand in as the nearest documented Zeiss Ikon site.
stops.campa: Conscripted with the rest of the closed theatres, Hoyer is sent to a branch of the Zeiss Ikon optical works in Dresden and put to war production. The firm makes lenses and range-finders and camera shutters, and by 1944 it makes them with labour it did not hire. She spends the autumn and the winter there. Which branch, and which shop floor, the surviving papers do not say. It is the only stretch of her adult life in which she is not, in some capacity, dancing.
suggested_refs: The Zeiss Ikon Ernemann works, Schandauer Strasse 76, Dresden, and its wartime conscripted labour
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Blasewitz, the cellar under the firestorm
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln places her in a Blasewitz cellar on the night of 13-14 February 1945. Coordinate corrected to the centre of Blasewitz from the dossier's 51.0311/13.7897.
stops.campa: On the night of the thirteenth of February the bombers come over Dresden in waves and the city burns for two days. Hoyer is in Blasewitz, in the cellar of people she knows, east of the old town and outside the worst of the firestorm. The Altstadt goes, and with it the theatres she has worked in and the schools that trained her. The Wigman house on the Bautzner Strasse, high above the river, stands. When the all-clear finally sounds she walks up the cellar steps into a district that is still there.
suggested_refs: The bombing of Dresden, 13-14 February 1945, survived by Hoyer in a Blasewitz cellar
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Bautzner Strasse, the Dore-Hoyer-Studio opens
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1945; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from mary_wigman.journey.json, which pins the school to Bautzner Strasse 107.
stops.campa: Four months after the fire Hoyer moves into the empty Wigman school on the Bautzner Strasse, the villa above the Elbe where a generation of German dancers was formed, and opens the Dore-Hoyer-Studio inside it. Mary Wigman has gone west; the rooms are standing; the city needs something. Til Thiele and Nora Friedrich teach beside her, Ulrich Kessler plays and composes, and a young dancer called Ursula Cain becomes the closest of the pupils. For three years Hoyer runs an institution.
suggested_refs: The Villa Wigman, Bautzner Strasse 107, Dresden, taken over as the Dore-Hoyer-Studio in June 1945
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Bautzner Strasse, dances for Käthe Kollwitz
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed, not resolved: the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln dates the cycle 1945, other summaries 1946. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The background dossier's added claim that Hoyer dedicated the cycle to the Communist Party is supported by no reachable source and has been dropped.
stops.campa: Out of the students' own improvisations and Kessler's music the studio builds Tänze für Käthe Kollwitz: motherhood, hunger, war, death, made by young women in a city where all four are the weather. The movement is heavy and low and close to the ground, worked against the black sheets the Dresden graphic artist made of the same subjects. It is the last new thing the studio makes that the authorities like. Does the cycle belong to 1945 or to 1946? The archive gives one year and the summaries give the other, and no document settles it.
suggested_refs: Käthe Kollwitz's graphic cycles on war, hunger and motherhood, against which the 1946 dances are built
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, Der grosse Gesang and the charge of formalism
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1947 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which records the formalism charge from Soviet-zone authorities; month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: The next cycle is hers again: Der grosse Gesang, five parts, danced alone. The cultural officers of the Soviet zone read it and call it formalism, the standing charge against work that is subjective, abstract and about nothing collective. Socialist realism is arriving and wants a dance that shows workers. The critics in the West will shortly call this the most complete work of art made on the German dance stage; the officers in Dresden call it a fault. What Hoyer's dance shows is one woman on a bare stage with a piano.
suggested_refs: Der grosse Gesang, five-part solo cycle, 1947, and the Soviet-zone formalism dispute
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, leaving the Soviet zone
stops.date_confidence: the departure and its political cause are attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; de.wikipedia supplies September 1948. The day is unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: The SED wants choreography made for its objectives, and says so. Hoyer, thirty-six, hands over nothing. She has now lost, in thirteen years, a partner, a city, a school and every institution she has been inside. Where she sleeps in the months between the leaving and the first Western engagement is not recorded anywhere reachable. In September she goes out of Dresden and the Soviet zone for good, three years after opening the studio, and the studio closes behind her.
suggested_refs: SED cultural policy in the Soviet zone, 1947-48, and the pressure on Dresden's independent dance
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Augsburg, guest evenings in the American zone
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1948 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which places Augsburg between Dresden and Hamburg; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to follow the September departure.
stops.campa: The first Western ground under her is Bavaria: guest performances at Augsburg, in the American zone, a city bombed about as thoroughly as the one she has left. She is a refugee with a repertoire. Nothing here is a post; they are evenings, arranged one at a time, in a currency reformed four months earlier and a country with no dance institutions left standing. Hoyer is thirty-six and starting again in the only profession she has. From Augsburg she goes north, because the north is where the offer is.
suggested_refs: Hoyer's 1948 Augsburg guest performances, the intermediate step between Dresden and Hamburg
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Hamburgische Staatsoper, engaged by Günther Rennert
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1949 by the Sächsische Biografie, the NDB and the Tanzarchiv; the month is the conventional season opening and is defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Dammtorstrasse from the dossier's 53.5637/9.9908.
stops.campa: Günther Rennert, rebuilding the Hamburg State Opera into the most ambitious house in the western zones, engages Hoyer as soloist and ballet mistress. The house is willing to be interested in her, and is not built for what she means to do in it. It is the largest institutional position she will ever hold, and she takes it with a plan: to turn an opera ballet, an apparatus that exists to fill the dance minutes of other people's operas, into a modern dance ensemble with a repertoire of its own.
suggested_refs: Günther Rennert's intendancy at the Hamburgische Staatsoper from 1946
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Hamburgische Staatsoper, Der Fremde
stops.date_confidence: attested for February 1950 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. The quotation is a Spanish translation at one remove, printed in Patricia Dorin's paper from Durante/Falcoff 2008; Hoyer's German original was not located.
stops.campa: In February she puts three group works on the Hamburg stage, the largest of them Der Fremde, a death-dance about a man his society casts out; the critics measure it against Kurt Jooss's Der grüne Tisch and it holds. But the ballet lives on the opera's calendar, rehearsing between Verdi and Wagner, and a repertoire cannot be built in the gaps. That April she sets down, for whoever is reading, what is coming back into the German theatres in place of the dance she makes.
stops.quote: ¿Por qué el ballet clásico vuelve a festejar victorias? Francia, Rusia, Inglaterra mandan a sus conjuntos a la Alemania hambrienta de grandes ballets. Y los devotos alemanes son marionetas agradecidas. A lo largo y a lo ancho soy la única coreógrafa de Danza Moderna, ultramoderna.
stops.quote_source: Dore Hoyer, statement of April 1950, in Spanish translation, quoted in Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina', citing Durante/Falcoff 2008:258
suggested_refs: Der Fremde (1950), read by critics against Kurt Jooss's Der grüne Tisch
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography
Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina'

stops.name: Hamburg, the resignation and the critics' prize
stops.date_confidence: the February 1951 resignation is attested by the Sächsische Biografie and the prize by the Sächsische Biografie and the NDB; the day is unrecorded and defaulted. The jury citation reaches this file only through de.wikipedia citing Müller/Peter/Schuldt 1992, p. 45; one verification pass reported that article carrying no such wording, and the monograph was not seen.
stops.campa: In February she resigns. The modern ensemble has not happened and will not; the opera ballet goes back to being an opera ballet. She has, in the same year, the best notices in the country and no company, no house and no salary; the two things are printed weeks apart and nobody in the profession finds the combination strange. Within months the Deutscher Kritikerpreis für Tanzkunst is given to her, and the jury sets down the highest sentence written about a German dancer that decade.
stops.quote: Unter allen deutschen Tänzerinnen der Nachkriegszeit ist Dore Hoyer die stärkste Persönlichkeit, und sie hat mit ihrer fünfteiligen Suite Der große Gesang als Solistin das bedeutendste und geschlossenste Kunstwerk auf der Tanzbühne geschaffen.
stops.quote_source: Citation of the Deutscher Kritikerpreis für Tanzkunst, 1951, quoted in the German Wikipedia article 'Dore Hoyer' citing Müller/Peter/Schuldt, Dore Hoyer. Tänzerin (Hentrich, Berlin 1992), p. 45; the monograph itself was not consulted
suggested_refs: The 1951 Deutscher Kritikerpreis für Tanzkunst and its jury citation
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Mannheim, Joan of Arc in a cinema
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1952 by the Tanzarchiv and de.wikipedia; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate is Mannheim city centre by deliberate choice: the Nationaltheater's Goetheplatz house was built 1955-57, so in 1952 the company was playing out of the Schauburg cinema in block K 1, its Schillerplatz house having been destroyed on 5 September 1943. The quotation's original letter, essay or interview is not named by the source that carries it.
stops.campa: Mannheim takes her as a guest to choreograph and direct Claudel and Honegger's Jeanne d'Arc au bûcher. The National Theatre has no theatre: its Schillerplatz house was destroyed in September 1943 and the company plays out of a converted cinema in block K 1 while a new building is argued over. Hoyer works inside somebody else's institution again, on somebody else's oratorio, and watches the pointe shoe and the tap shoe come back into the German houses that do not employ her.
stops.quote: Hoch leben Spitze und Stepp. Damit ist die letzte Chance für den heutigen Tanz verloren.
stops.quote_source: Dore Hoyer, quoted in Laura Bettag, 'Zeitfenster Nr. 50: Dore Hoyer', Nationaltheater Mannheim; the page names no letter, essay or date for the remark
suggested_refs: Claudel and Honegger's Jeanne d'Arc au bûcher, staged at Mannheim in 1952
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography
Laura Bettag, 'Zeitfenster Nr. 50: Dore Hoyer', Nationaltheater Mannheim

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first South American tour
stops.date_confidence: the 1952 Argentina and Brazil tour with Wiatowitsch is attested by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, which also records regular South American tours through 1963; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The Teatro Colon as a venue of this tour is reconstruction only: the page the background dossier cited for it contains nothing on Argentina at all. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Buenos Aires city pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: She and Wiatowitsch cross the Atlantic and find, in Argentina and Brazil, the audience Germany has stopped being. Buenos Aires in 1952 has money, theatres, a European emigration and an appetite for exactly the severe solo evening the Hamburg critics praised and the Hamburg public did not fill a house for. She will come back five more times over eleven years. The Teatro Colon is named as a venue of this first tour, though by no document now reachable. What she writes on getting home is not about the triumph.
stops.quote: La danza expresiva ha pasado de moda; el público quiere alegría, bromas, risas. Mi danza es manifestación de duelo. ¿Para qué voy a agobiar al público con mi duelo? No voy a bailar, no más!
stops.quote_source: Dore Hoyer, on returning to Germany after her first South American tour, c. 1952-53, in Spanish translation, quoted in Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina', citing Durante/Falcoff 2008:260
suggested_refs: The 1952 Argentina and Brazil tour with Dimitri Wiatowitsch, first of six South American tours to 1963
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography
Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina'

stops.name: Ulm, the year of the knee
stops.date_confidence: the Ulm guest work and the 1954 accident are both attested for the year, the accident by de.wikipedia and indirectly by the NDB; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The two are placed together for order only: no source connects the injury to Ulm, and its place, day and circumstances are undocumented.
stops.campa: A guest season at Ulm, a small house with a large idea of itself. Somewhere in this same year there is an accident, and a knee is injured that does not heal. No source names the day, the place or how it happened. She is forty-two, thirteen years from her last performance, and every one of the thirteen is danced on it. From here the pain medication is part of the preparation for an evening. In the estate at Cologne there is an X-ray of the knee, and nothing else at all about it.
suggested_refs: The knee X-ray preserved in Bestand 001, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Athens, guest work and an Elektra
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1956 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Kreutzberg's Moira von Mykene is dated to the same year but its performance venue is not established, and it is named here rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Athens engages her as guest choreographer and performer. The same year brings Harald Kreutzberg's Moira von Mykene, in which she dances Elektra: two Greek commissions inside twelve months for a dancer whose German bookings are thinning. What she made in Athens, and for whom, the reachable sources do not say. She is forty-four and works the way guests work, one contract at a time, in whatever country will pay for the evening. Neither Greek commission leads to a post.
suggested_refs: Harald Kreutzberg's Moira von Mykene (1956), with Hoyer as Elektra
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: New London, the American Dance Festival
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1957 and for six weeks at the tenth American Dance Festival; the month follows the festival's usual summer season and is defaulted. The quotation's German is confirmed in the de.wikipedia raw wikitext; its ultimate source is Müller/Peter/Schuldt 1992, p. 59, which was not seen. The reported New York studio visits are reconstruction, no address being itemised anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: Mary Wigman secures her the invitation, and Hoyer crosses to America for six weeks at the tenth American Dance Festival, on a Connecticut campus above the Thames river. She watches Martha Graham's technique, Doris Humphrey's, José Limón's, and finds most of what she sees only motoric, dramatic and grotesque, short on feeling and on quiet and on whatever is intimate; Limón and his group she excepts. About New York itself she has no reservations at all.
stops.quote: die Hochburg des modernen Tanzes, wie es das in Deutschland nicht mehr gibt
stops.quote_source: Dore Hoyer on New York, quoted in the German Wikipedia article 'Dore Hoyer' citing Müller/Peter/Schuldt, Dore Hoyer. Tänzerin (Hentrich, Berlin 1992), p. 59; the monograph itself was not consulted
suggested_refs: The tenth American Dance Festival, Connecticut College, New London, summer 1957
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

segments.name: The Chosen One, and La Plata

stops.name: Berlin, the Chosen One in Le Sacre du printemps
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln gives September 1957 and de.wikipedia's Mary Wigman article names the Städtische Oper, which between 1945 and September 1961 played in the Theater des Westens. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from mary_wigman.journey.json. The quotation's German original, date and occasion are attested nowhere reachable.
stops.campa: Mary Wigman, seventy, stages Stravinsky's Sacre du printemps for the Berlin Festwochen at the Städtische Oper, forty-five dancers on the stage of the Theater des Westens, and gives the Chosen One to Hoyer. Hoyer is forty-five and has spent twenty-two years being called Wigman's pupil, which she was not. The role is a woman danced to death by her own tribe so that the year will turn, and the ovation on the night belongs to the old woman in the wings. On the twenty-fourth of September she dances the sacrifice.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman on Dore Hoyer, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Dore Hoyer' citing Karen Bell-Kanner, The Life and Times of Ellen von Frankenberg (1991), p. 118; no German original, date or occasion is attested in any reachable source
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman's Le Sacre du printemps, Berlin Festwochen 1957, reconstructed 2013 by Tanzfonds Erbe
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Berlin, the dances round the golden calf
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed, not resolved: the Neue Deutsche Biographie dates the work 1958, de.wikipedia attaches it to the 1959 German premiere. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The house is uncertain for the same reason as the 1957 stop, the opera company still playing in the Theater des Westens until September 1961; the pin is deliberately identical.
stops.campa: For a West Berlin production connected with Schoenberg's Moses und Aron she makes Tänze um das goldene Kalb, the dance of the people around the idol while the lawgiver is up the mountain. The dating is not settled: the Neue Deutsche Biographie puts it in 1958, other summaries attach it to the German premiere of 1959. The house is not settled either, the opera company still playing in the Theater des Westens and not opening its own building on the Bismarckstrasse until September 1961.
suggested_refs: Tänze um das goldene Kalb, for a West Berlin production of Schoenberg's Moses und Aron

stops.name: La Plata, the movement choir on the Rio de la Plata
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln records the movement choir and chamber group, and es.wikipedia's Oscar Araiz article independently confirms both the teaching and the Grupo Camara. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Teatro Argentino on Calle 10 from the dossier's -34.9187/-57.9545. The quotation is an eyewitness's words about Hoyer, not Hoyer's own.
stops.campa: The cultural administration of Buenos Aires Province hires her to build a modern dance ensemble at the Teatro Argentino de La Plata, and she builds two: a chamber group, and a larger Coro de Movimiento, the German movement choir transplanted to the Rio de la Plata. This is the closest Hoyer comes to having a company again, and it is on another continent, in a language she does not speak. Among the students is Oscar Araiz, who joins her Grupo Camara and will carry Argentine modern dance for the next forty years.
stops.quote: (…) Era la primera vez que iba a ver un espectáculo de Danza Moderna…Tuve una especie de shock emocional, no pude para de llorar en toda la función y cada cosa que veía era más impacto, más impresión, más fuerte y salí preguntándome ¿y esto existía? Eso era lo que yo siempre hubiera querido hacer…
stops.quote_source: Susana Zimermann, Argentine choreographer, recalling a Hoyer performance in Buenos Aires, quoted in Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina', citing Issemoyano 2006:84
suggested_refs: The Coro de Movimiento and Grupo Camara at the Teatro Argentino de La Plata, c. 1960-62
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography
Patricia Dorin, 'Filiaciones y derivaciones de una danza de expresion en la Argentina'

stops.name: Berlin, the five passions after Spinoza
stops.date_confidence: the work, its five titles, its Spinoza source and the Wiatowitsch score are attested for 1962; the return to Germany that year is attested by the Tanzarchiv, though the motives the background dossier gave for it are unsourced and dropped. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. A declared central Berlin coordinate: no source names the room the cycle was made in.
stops.campa: She returns to Germany in 1962, though not out of Argentina entirely, and makes the work everything else will be measured against. Affectos Humanos: five solos to Wiatowitsch's score, taking their names and their order from Spinoza's account of the passions. Honour and Vanity. Desire. Hatred. Fear. Love. Fear reuses the knee-striking figure out of her Der Schrei of 1936, twenty-six years carried forward into a new grammar. Hamburg's Freie Akademie der Künste elects her a member the same year. She is fifty.
suggested_refs: Affectos Humanos (1962), music by Dimitri Wiatowitsch, reconstructed by Susanne Linke in 1987 and by Arila Siegert in 1989
sources: Tanzfonds Erbe, 'Affectos Humanos by Dore Hoyer' (Nils Freyer documentation)
Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Akademie der Künste, the solo from Dostoevsky
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1964 by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The Hanseatenweg address is institutional record rather than a documented residence, and the sources describe the arrangement only loosely.
stops.campa: From 1964 the West Berlin Akademie der Künste on the Hanseatenweg is her base and, in the loose sense the sources use, her address. A dancer of fifty-two performing a monologue about a suicide, in a room lent by an academy, is what the German dance profession has left for its most decorated soloist. The solo she makes there is out of Dostoevsky's Die Sanfte, a husband talking beside the body of the young wife who threw herself out of a window. It succeeds.
suggested_refs: Die Sanfte, after Dostoevsky's A Gentle Creature, solo of c. 1964
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Akademie der Künste, Grossstadt and the second failure
stops.date_confidence: the work is attested for 1965; that it failed is reconstruction, carried by the background dossier and not reconfirmed by any source fetched. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: She tries for a company once more, at fifty-three. Grossstadt is an ensemble work, the big city as its subject, Hoyer dancing in it herself, and it does not take. This is the second attempt after Hamburg and the last. The tradition she is the end of has no students in it. There is no money and no house, and no younger generation of German dancers formed in the vocabulary the piece needs: the ones who might have been were trained after 1945 in ballet.
suggested_refs: Grossstadt (1965), Hoyer's last attempt at a free ensemble
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Delhi, the Goethe-Institut tour
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed and weighted: the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln gives autumn 1965 specifically, the Sächsische Biografie a bare 1966; the specific attestation anchors the date and 1966 is the variant. The day is unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate is a declared placeholder: no reachable source names a single city or hall on the itinerary, only the regions.
stops.campa: In the autumn the Goethe-Institut sends her east: Southeast Asia, East Asia, India, a solo dancer of fifty-three carrying her own repertoire and her own accompanist through a run of cultural-diplomacy engagements. The German state that will not build her a company will pay to show her abroad. One biography dates the whole tour a year later than the archive does, and neither of them says when she came home. No source now reachable names the cities or the halls, only the regions.
suggested_refs: Goethe-Institut records of the 1965 Southeast Asia, East Asia and India tour
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Affectos Humanos on tape
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That a Hessischer Rundfunk recording of Affectos Humanos exists is supported by de.wikipedia's reference to 'die Filmaufzeichnung des HR', but the page the background dossier cited carries no broadcaster, no 15 February 1967 date, no issue date and no credits, so all of those are stripped. Frankfurt is the broadcaster's home city; no source names the studio. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: Hessischer Rundfunk films Affectos Humanos in black and white. It is the only substantial moving record of Hoyer dancing her own choreography, and every reconstruction attempted since has had to work from it. She is fifty-five and dances the five passions on a knee thirteen years injured, in a television studio, for a fee. The exact date, the studio, the credits and the broadcast title are given differently by different summaries and confirmed by none of the documents now reachable. Ten months later she is dead.
suggested_refs: The Hessischer Rundfunk recording of Affectos Humanos, the source film for the reconstructions by Susanne Linke (1987), Arila Siegert (1989), Betsy Fisher (1995-97) and Nils Freyer (2018)
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography
Tanzfonds Erbe, 'Affectos Humanos by Dore Hoyer' (Nils Freyer documentation)

stops.name: Theater des Westens, the last evening
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly by the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln and de.wikipedia, including the self-financing, the attendance of a little over one hundred, and the topical piece Vietnam. Coordinate deliberately identical to the 1957 Sacre stop: the same building, inherited byte-identical from mary_wigman.journey.json, reconciling the two divergent values the background dossier carried.
stops.campa: She rents the Theater des Westens herself, at her own cost, prints the bills and advertises it herself. It is a large West Berlin house, and on the eighteenth of December a little over a hundred people come to it. The programme includes Vietnam, a new piece about the war. She dances the evening on pain medication, in the same building where she was Wigman's Chosen One ten years earlier, to a room that is empty in every direction she can see from the stage.
suggested_refs: Vietnam, Hoyer's last new work, premiered at her self-financed evening of 18 December 1967
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: West Berlin, the poison brought from South America
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested for 31 December 1967 by the NDB, the Sächsische Biografie and the Tanzarchiv independently; machine-readable catalogues give 30 December, a divergence printed and not adjudicated. The December 1967 second Kritikerpreis is attested by the Tanzarchiv. The quotation is reconstruction: the letter is untraced and the English is a translation at one remove. The apartment is unrecorded, so a declared central coordinate is used.
stops.campa: In December the critics give her the Deutscher Kritikerpreis a second time, sixteen years after the first. It changes nothing: the debt from the Theater des Westens stands, the knee stands, the profession has no place for her. On the night of the thirty-first she writes her farewell letters and takes poison she had brought back from South America years before and kept. Most authorities give the thirty-first of December. Some catalogue records give the thirtieth.
stops.quote: Only in dance could I communicate.
stops.quote_source: Dore Hoyer, from one of her last letters, as quoted in Isa Partsch-Bergsohn, Modern Dance in Germany and the United States (1994), p. 122, via the English Wikipedia article 'Dore Hoyer'; the letter itself is untraced and page 122 was not seen
suggested_refs: Hoyer's farewell letters, preserved in Bestand 001, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Frankfurter Hauptfriedhof, the grave nobody explains
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Frankfurt's main cemetery is attested by the Tanzarchiv and de.wikipedia; the date of interment is unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Eckenheimer Landstrasse from two different wrong values the background dossier carried for the same grave. The cemetery's own article does not list her among its notable burials.
stops.campa: She is buried in the main cemetery of Frankfurt am Main, on the Eckenheimer Landstrasse. The cemetery's own register of notable graves does not list her. A bronze bust of her by Bernhard Heiliger sits in a private collection somewhere in the same city, and nobody publishes the address of the room it stands in. She was born in Dresden, worked in Hamburg and Berlin, and had no documented life in Frankfurt at all. Why Frankfurt, then? No biography now reachable explains it.
suggested_refs: Bernhard Heiliger's bronze bust of Dore Hoyer, private collection, Frankfurt am Main
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Köln, Bestand 001 of the German Dance Archive
stops.date_confidence: the estate's contents and its catalogue number are attested by the archive's own finding aid; the year of deposit is not stated in any reachable source and the date here orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The estate goes to Cologne, a city she is not known to have worked in, and is catalogued as Bestand 001 of the German Dance Archive: notebooks, correspondence, the farewell letters, costumes, scores, sound recordings, photographs, tax papers and medical records. She published no book, no diary, no collected letters, no recording under her own name. Everything she wrote that survives is in those boxes, and so is the copyright to every choreography and every text she made.
suggested_refs: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, finding aid 'Bestandsuebersicht 001 Dore Hoyer'
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, finding aid 'Bestandsuebersicht 001 Dore Hoyer'
Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Dore Hoyer estate biography

stops.name: Dresden, a street by the Grosser Garten
stops.date_confidence: the street is attested by de.wikipedia and the Sächsische Biografie, but no reachable source gives the year of dedication; the date here is a declared placeholder that orders the segment only. Coordinate from OSM, correcting the background dossier's 51.04/13.79, which lands in Gruna three kilometres east.
stops.campa: Dresden names a street after her: Dore-Hoyer-Strasse, in the Seevorstadt-Ost beside the Grosser Garten, a short residential run in the 01069 postal district. It lies about half a kilometre from the Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, where she performed in public for the first time in 1930 and collected a teacher's diploma she never used. The city that burned around her and then expelled her keeps her name on a signpost near the building where she started. What year the name went up, nobody has written down where it can now be read.
suggested_refs: Dore-Hoyer-Strasse, Seevorstadt-Ost, 01069 Dresden
